title: Per-query adaptive precision fallbacks and clock-slew policy for heterogeneous GPU fleets
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note sketches a practical approach to reducing tail latency and cost for live inference by combining per-query precision fallbacks (precision/quantization-selective kernels) with a cautious GPU clock-slew and soft power-capping policy. The goal is to allow the runtime to: (1) degrade arithmetic precision or kernel fidelity on a per-request basis when appropriate, (2) move GPU clock/power state gradually in response to workload pulses to avoid thermal/QoS instability, and (3) coordinate these behaviours with KV cache warming/placement and scheduler priorities across heterogeneous fleets (A100/H100/L4/MI300).

This is an engineering-first draft — contains heuristics, open questions, and an experimental rollout plan. Not a final spec.

Motivation (short):
- Observation: peak microbursts (short bursts of high concurrency) often cause tail latency spikes and force conservative fleet-wide clocking policies that lower average throughput.
- Fine-grained model-level quantization/precision choices (FP16 -> INT8 or BF16->FP16 mixed kernels) can reduce per-token runtime and memory pressure but sometimes introduce visible quality regressions.
- A policy that combines prediction-driven, per-query precision fallback with a slow, constrained clock-slew prevents thermal/QoS thrash while enabling transient high-performance operation.

Design principles:
- Safety-first: precision fallback must be reversible and constrained by per-model fidelity budgets (we keep per-model eval thresholds; see telemetry below).
- Predictive and conservative clock changes: never jump clocks across big steps for single queries; apply limited headroom changes with backoff windows.
- Scheduler-aware: prioritize warm-KV and long lived sessions when choosing higher clocks or higher-fidelity kernels.
- Observability: expose per-request precision decisions and clock transitions in traces and aggregates.

Components overview:
1) Per-query Precision Selector (PQPS)
- Input signals: model id, model version, sequence length (prompt + expected gen), user QoS class, recent eval/fidelity score for that model, request importance flag (from application), and recent per-GPU thermal/power headroom.
- Decision outputs: kernel profile (e.g., fp16-standard, int8-fast, bf16-safe), target per-layer quantization map (optional), and an explicit quality budget token (used for rollout accounting).
- Policies:
  - Default: serve fp16/bf16 for current verified models.
  - If predicted latency risk > threshold AND model has remaining fidelity budget, select int8-fast for non-critical requests or for short-response queries (length < 64).
  - For gen-heavy queries (expected tokens > 256) prioritize memory-friendly kernels (kv-sliced, chunked matmul) over extreme quantization.
- Implementation note: PQPS runs in the front-end router to avoid wasted compute; decisions are cached keyed by (model, prompt-token-hash, QoS).

2) Clock-slew manager (CSM)
- Goal: allow small, fast-perceptible increases in GPU clocks for short windows without triggering wide thermal oscillation or eviction cascades.
- Policy parameters: step_size (% clock or MHz), max_steps_per_window, cooldown_ms, per-GPU thermal_guard (degrees C), sustained_power_limit_w, transient_power_budget_w.
- Behaviour: on detection of microburst or high-priority warm-KV requests, the CSM may request up to N incremental steps; each step is applied after verifying thermal_guard and existing throttles. If temperature rises > delta_T, CSM backs off and performs a staged cooldown.
- Hardware-specific knobs: e.g., H100 supports finer power granularity; L4 often requires coarser steps and is more sensitive to memory-clock changes. MI300 thermal inertia higher but peak power cap affects sustained throughput.

3) KV Cache placement and prefetcher coordination
- When PQPS chooses higher fidelity kernels that increase KV residency, scheduler should prefer nodes with warmed KV or trigger asynchronous prefetch into GPU memory when prefetch budget allows.
- For int8-fast kernels that reduce per-token compute, KV cache pressure might actually increase (more simultaneous sequences). In that case, prefer KV-slice placement that minimizes total DRAM->HBM transfers for the hot shard.

4) Scheduler integration (per-node and global)
- Scheduler decisions consider: (a) PQPS kernel choice, (b) CSM current headroom, (c) KV warm score, (d) request QoS.
- Simple score function (heuristic):
  score = w_qos*QoS_priority + w_kv*KV_warm_score + w_fid*(fidelity_penalty) + w_headroom*(available_headroom)
  - If score above launch threshold, request is scheduled on high-clock pool; otherwise routed to baseline pool or a lower-fidelity kernel.
- Preemption: allow soft preemption where long-running low-priority jobs can be throttled first during headroom exhaustion (rather than evicting warm-KV).

Telemetry and fidelity accounting:
- Record per-request: decided kernel, model-version, predicted vs actual latency, quality metrics if available, fidelity-budget-consumed, GPU clock before/after, temperature and power draw.
- Aggregates: 95/99/99.9 latency by kernel type and model, quality regression alerts (e.g., BLEU/SARI/ROUGE drops for benchmark prompts), and per-model fidelity budget consumption rate.
- Alerts: unexpected quality regression for any model -> immediate rollback of PQPS rules for that model.

Open questions and edge cases:
- How to evaluate quality for open-ended models in production? Proposal: maintain a representative prompt set per model and sample a small % of live traffic for offline eval daily.
- Interaction with autoscaler: aggressive clocking may increase throughput and trigger autoscaler reactions. Need to place a cap on autoscaler decisions tied to clock budget window.
- Heterogeneous fleets: how to encode capability metadata so router picks a pool compatible with PQPS kernel (e.g., L4 lacks optimized int8 path for some ops).
- Security: ensure PQPS decisions do not leak model eval metrics across tenants.

Experiments to run (short list):
- A/B test: baseline (no PQPS, static clocks) vs PQPS + conservative CSM on subset of fleet for a set of 10 models (mix of chat & code models). Metric: 99.9 latency, quantized to cost per 1k tokens, and manual QA on sampled outputs.
- Thermal stress test: synthetic microburst load while toggling step_size and cooldown_ms to measure thermal oscillation and system SLO impact.
- KV prefetch tradeoff: quantify latency impact when prefetch budget is set to 0%, 5%, 15% of network bandwidth for warm-KV traffic.

Rollout plan (experimental -> staged):
- Stage 0 (lab): run PQPS + CSM in canary cluster with disabled autoscaler; verify thermal stability and regression metrics.
- Stage 1 (internal dev): enable on small percentage of production traffic for non-critical tenants; use conservative fidelity budgets.
- Stage 2 (opt-in customers): allow enterprise customers to opt-in for performance tiers, expose fidelity budget and per-model rollback toggle.

Implementation TODOs and tickets (rough):
- PQPS proto routing hook + cache (INF-1843).
- Kernel mapping registry: map model ops -> supported kernels per GPU type.
- CSM agent with stepper and safety checks + per-node telemetry.
- Scheduler scoring change with affinity table and soft preemption.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally heuristic-heavy; I think practical gains will come from combining lightweight prediction (PQPS) with conservative hardware changes.
- Prioritize visibility: add detailed counters for each decision, so rollbacks are fast if regressions appear.
- Please add thoughts re: specific kernel names we should expose as policy knobs (Rafael/PRiya to propose mapping for H100 and L4).
